questions.topic: Sample Space and Types of Events
questions.question: A fair coin is tossed once. Let \( S \) denote the sample space of this experiment. Find \( n(S) \).
questions.explanation:
The sample space \( S \) lists every possible outcome of the experiment.

Counting all of them gives \( n(S)=2 \).

distractor_logic: Comes from counting only one face of the coin, forgetting the coin has two possible outcomes.
Comes from miscounting the outcomes of a coin toss as three instead of two.
Comes from confusing this experiment with tossing two coins, which has 4 outcomes.

questions.explanation: The classical definition of probability, for equally likely outcomes, is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes: \( P(A)=\dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)} \).

topics.name: Sample Space and Types of Events
topics.summary: Probability begins with a random experiment: a process whose result cannot be predicted with certainty in advance, though every possible result is known beforehand. The sample space \( S \) is the set of all possible outcomes of such an experiment, and an event is simply a subset of \( S \). Events come in several types: a simple (or elementary) event contains exactly one outcome of \( S \); a compound event contains more than one; the sure event equals the whole of \( S \) itself, since it is certain to happen; and the impossible event is \( \phi \), the empty set, since it can never happen. For combined experiments — tossing several coins, rolling several dice, or drawing several items in sequence — the sample space is built using the multiplication principle: multiply the number of outcomes at each stage together, adjusting later stages when earlier draws are not replaced. Getting \( n(S) \) right is the essential first step before any probability can be computed.
key_formulas: \( S = \) the set of all possible outcomes of a random experiment
\( n(S) = \) total number of outcomes (multiply outcome-counts stage by stage for combined experiments)
topics.worked_example: For the experiment of tossing three fair coins together, each toss has 2 outcomes, so \( n(S)=2\times2\times2=8 \), and \( S=\{HHH,HHT,HTH,THH,HTT,THT,TTH,TTT\} \). The event 'exactly two heads' is \( \{HHT,HTH,THH\} \), a compound event with 3 outcomes; the event 'all three heads' is \( \{HHH\} \), a simple event with exactly one outcome.
common_mistakes: Adding the outcome-counts of each stage instead of multiplying them (e.g. treating two dice as \( 6+6 \) instead of \( 6\times6 \))
Forgetting that drawing without replacement shrinks the outcome-count of later stages
Miscounting a simple event as compound (or vice versa) by not checking exactly how many outcomes of \( S \) the event actually contains

topics.name: Algebra of Events — Union, Intersection and Complement
topics.summary: Since events are sets of outcomes, the usual set operations describe how events combine. The union \( A \cup B \) is the event that \( A \) or \( B \) (or both) occurs — every outcome in \( A \), in \( B \), or in both, listed once each. The intersection \( A \cap B \) is the event that both \( A \) and \( B \) occur together — only the outcomes shared by both sets. The complement \( A' \) is the event that \( A \) does NOT occur — every outcome of \( S \) left out of \( A \), so \( n(A')=n(S)-n(A) \). Two useful identities (De Morgan's laws) connect these operations: \( (A\cup B)'=A'\cap B' \) and \( (A\cap B)'=A'\cup B' \). Also, for any event \( A \), \( A\cap A'=\phi \) and \( A\cup A'=S \) always hold, since every outcome of \( S \) is in exactly one of \( A \) or \( A' \), never both and never neither.
key_formulas: \( A \cup B = \) outcomes in \( A \), or \( B \), or both
\( A \cap B = \) outcomes in both \( A \) and \( B \)
common_mistakes: Adding \( n(A) \) and \( n(B) \) directly for the union without removing outcomes double-counted in \( A\cap B \)
Confusing \( A\cap B \) with \( A\cup B \), or reporting one when the other was asked
Forgetting to switch to the complement \( A' \) — reporting \( n(A) \) or \( n(S) \) instead of \( n(S)-n(A) \)

topics.name: Probability of an Event — Equally Likely Outcomes
topics.summary: When every outcome of a sample space \( S \) is equally likely, the classical (theoretical) probability of an event \( A \) is defined as the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes: \( P(A) = \dfrac{n(A)}{n(S)} \). Every probability satisfies \( 0 \leq P(A) \leq 1 \): the impossible event has \( P(\phi)=0 \), and the sure event has \( P(S)=1 \), since \( n(S)/n(S)=1 \). For combined or repeated experiments, the classical formula still applies directly once the combined sample space is correctly established, and for successive draws WITH replacement, the probability of a repeated outcome is found by multiplying the single-draw probability by itself. For larger sample spaces — several balls or cards drawn together, where order does not matter — combinations \( \binom{n}{r} \) are used to count both the favourable ways and the total ways before forming the same ratio.
key_formulas: For \( r \) items drawn together from \( n \) (order irrelevant): counts use \( \binom{n}{r} \)
topics.worked_example: A bag contains 4 red and 6 white balls; two balls are drawn together at random. The total ways to choose 2 from 9 is \( n(S)=\binom{9}{2}=36 \). The ways to choose 2 red balls is \( n(A)=\binom{4}{2}=6 \). So \( P(\text{both red})=\dfrac{6}{36}=\dfrac{1}{6} \).
common_mistakes: Inverting the ratio, computing \( n(S)/n(A) \) instead of \( n(A)/n(S) \)
Miscounting the sample space of a combined experiment (e.g. using 6 instead of 36 for two dice)
Using permutations where order does not matter, or combinations where it does, when counting favourable or total outcomes

topics.name: Mutually Exclusive and Exhaustive Events
topics.summary: Two events \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive if they cannot both occur on the same trial — they share no common outcome, so \( A\cap B=\phi \). This is checked directly: list (or count) \( A\cap B \), and if it is empty, the events are mutually exclusive. A collection of events is exhaustive if, together, they cover the entire sample space — every outcome of \( S \) belongs to at least one of them, so their union equals \( S \). A set of events can be mutually exclusive without being exhaustive (they might miss some outcomes), exhaustive without being mutually exclusive (they might overlap), both at once (a true partition of \( S \)), or neither. When a collection of events is both mutually exclusive and exhaustive, it forms a partition of the sample space: every outcome belongs to exactly one of the events, with none left over and none double-counted.
key_formulas: Exhaustive: \( A \cup B = S \) (for a full partition, \( E_1\cup E_2\cup\cdots\cup E_k=S \))
A partition of \( S \): mutually exclusive AND exhaustive together
topics.worked_example: A die is rolled once. Let \( E_1=\{1,2\} \), \( E_2=\{3,4\} \), \( E_3=\{5,6\} \). Checking pairwise, no two of these share an outcome, so they are mutually exclusive; and \( E_1\cup E_2\cup E_3=\{1,2,3,4,5,6\}=S \), so they are also exhaustive. Together, \( E_1,E_2,E_3 \) form a partition of \( S \).
common_mistakes: Concluding events are mutually exclusive just because they look different in description, without actually checking \( A\cap B \)
Confusing mutual exclusivity (about the intersection being empty) with exhaustiveness (about the union covering \( S \)) — they are separate checks
Assuming a set of events must be exhaustive simply because it is mutually exclusive, or vice versa

topics.name: Addition Theorem and the Probability of 'Not A'
topics.summary: The addition theorem gives the probability that \( A \) or \( B \) (or both) occurs: \( P(A\cup B) = P(A)+P(B)-P(A\cap B) \). The subtraction corrects for outcomes in \( A\cap B \), which would otherwise be counted twice by adding \( P(A) \) and \( P(B) \) directly. When \( A \) and \( B \) are mutually exclusive, \( P(A\cap B)=0 \), so the formula simplifies to the special case \( P(A\cup B)=P(A)+P(B) \). Every event \( A \) also has a complement \( A' \) (the event that \( A \) does not occur), with \( P(A')=1-P(A) \); this is often the fastest route to 'at least one' problems, since it is usually easier to find the probability that NONE of something happens and subtract from 1 than to count every 'at least one' case directly. 'Exactly one' problems, by contrast, are typically solved by splitting into cases and multiplying counts for each case before combining them.
key_formulas: \( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) - P(A \cap B) \) (general form)
\( P(A \cup B) = P(A) + P(B) \) (mutually exclusive events only)
topics.worked_example: A card is drawn from a standard deck. Let \( A \) be 'drawing a heart' (\( P(A)=\dfrac{13}{52} \)) and \( B \) be 'drawing a face card' (\( P(B)=\dfrac{12}{52} \)); these overlap in the 3 face-card hearts, so \( P(A\cap B)=\dfrac{3}{52} \). By the addition theorem, \( P(A\cup B)=\dfrac{13}{52}+\dfrac{12}{52}-\dfrac{3}{52}=\dfrac{22}{52}=\dfrac{11}{26} \).
common_mistakes: Applying the mutually-exclusive shortcut \( P(A)+P(B) \) to events that actually overlap, forgetting to subtract \( P(A\cap B) \)
Adding the overlap term \( P(A\cap B) \) instead of subtracting it
Trying to count 'at least one' outcomes directly instead of using the complement (finding 'none' first, then subtracting from 1)
